title: Streptococci and Enterococci: Hemolysis First, Then the Disks
summary: Identify catalase-negative Gram-positive cocci by hemolysis, then bacitracin, PYR, CAMP, hippurate, salt tolerance, bile esculin, optochin and bile solubility — and know why a negative rapid strep test in a child needs a backup.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 57 Hit 4 (group A), Hit 5 (group B, CAMP, screening window), Hit 6 (shared PYR positivity), Hits 8 and 23 (pneumococcus vs viridans) and Hit 29 (PYR-positive, bacitracin-resistant isolate) plus Trap 4 (rapid antigen sensitivity). Checked against Gajic 2026, Gebre 2024, Zhou 2023, Guo 2019, Shakir 2021, Attaway 2024, Devabhaktuni 2025, Aupaix 2025, Cohen 2012, Boyanton 2024 and Fialho 2026. Hit 29 calls Enterococcus a “β-hemolytic streptococcus”; most enterococci are not β-hemolytic (register flag rv-entero-beta). The reviewer gives rapid antigen sensitivity as 31–95%; the lesson teaches ≈ 85% overall, falling to ≈ 40% with a light inoculum (Cohen 2012). Not taught: rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis latency, bacitracin resistance of group B and enterococci (no source read).

objectives: Classify catalase-negative Gram-positive cocci by hemolysis pattern.
Separate group A, group B and Enterococcus with bacitracin, PYR, CAMP, hippurate, 6.5% NaCl and bile esculin.
Separate S. pneumoniae from viridans streptococci and name the limits of optochin and bile solubility.
Explain why a negative rapid group A antigen test in a child needs a backup test.

scenes.title: A negative rapid strep — and a plate that disagrees
scenes.altText: A throat swab from a 9-year-old with a sore throat. A rapid antigen strip shows only the control line: negative. A backup blood-agar plate (schematic) grows small colonies with clear halos. The Gram stain shows purple cocci in chains. Three question tokens: “Group A?”, “Group B?”, “Enterococcus?”. The cartoon scientist frowns at the strip.

cues.text: A 9-year-old has a sore throat. The rapid strep antigen test is negative, so a backup throat culture is set up.
The next day the blood agar shows small colonies with clear halos, and the Gram stain shows purple cocci in chains.
Was the rapid test wrong? And which chain-forming coccus is this? A few cheap tests will sort it out.

scenes.title: Sort 1: what the colony does to the blood
scenes.altText: After catalase (negative for streptococci and enterococci), the blood agar is read for hemolysis. Three schematic colonies: β — a clear, transparent halo (complete lysis); α — a greenish halo (partial lysis); γ — no change. Tokens drop under each: β → groups A and B; α → S. pneumoniae and viridans streptococci; γ → most enterococci. A note: enterococci are usually not β-hemolytic, though some strains are.

cues.text: Streptococci and enterococci are catalase negative. The next sort is hemolysis: what the colony does to the red cells in blood agar.
Beta hemolysis is a clear, transparent halo: the red cells are completely lysed. Group A and group B streptococci are beta.
Alpha hemolysis is a greenish halo from partial lysis. Streptococcus pneumoniae and the viridans streptococci are alpha.
Gamma means no change at all. Most enterococci look like this, although a minority of strains are beta.
Hemolysis narrows the list, but it never names the organism. That takes the disks and broths in the next steps.

props.title: Hemolysis narrows — it does not identify

scenes.title: Sort 2: the β-hemolytic split — bacitracin, PYR, CAMP, salt
scenes.altText: A schematic plate with a bacitracin disk: a group A colony lawn shows a clear zone (sensitive). A PYR token turns red/positive. Then the CAMP test: a straight vertical streak of S. aureus and a horizontal streak of group B streptococcus; an arrowhead of enhanced hemolysis grows where they meet. A hippurate token turns positive. Finally an organism that is PYR-positive but has no bacitracin zone is tested: it grows in 6.5% NaCl and turns bile esculin black → Enterococcus. A screening card: pregnant patients are screened for GBS at 36 0/7–37 6/7 weeks.

cues.text: Group A streptococcus, Streptococcus pyogenes, is bacitracin sensitive: a clear zone forms around the disk.
Group A is also PYR positive. But PYR alone is not enough, because enterococci are PYR positive too.
Group B, Streptococcus agalactiae, is CAMP positive. Its CAMP factor teams up with a staphylococcal toxin to make an arrowhead of stronger hemolysis.
Group B is also hippurate positive and PYR negative. Pregnant patients are screened for it at 36 to 37 weeks.
PYR positive with no bacitracin zone? Check salt and bile. Growth in 6.5% salt and a positive bile esculin test mean Enterococcus.

scenes.title: Pneumococcus vs viridans — and the rapid test explained
scenes.altText: Left: an α-hemolytic plate with an optochin (P) disk shows a zone for S. pneumoniae; a bile tube shows the pneumococcal cells dissolving (autolysis). A caution card: up to 18% of pneumococci are optochin resistant; some non-capsulated strains are bile insoluble; MALDI-TOF struggles with the S. mitis group; lytA PCR is the reference method; the Quellung reaction serotypes the capsule. Right: the rapid antigen test card: sensitivity ≈ 85%, falling to ≈ 40% with a light inoculum; negative results at ages 3–21 need a backup culture; rapid NAATs may replace the backup. The patient’s culture is group A.

cues.text: For alpha-hemolytic cocci, pneumococcus is optochin sensitive: a zone forms around the P disk. Viridans streptococci are resistant.
Pneumococcus is also bile soluble. Bile salts trigger its own autolysin, and the cells dissolve.
Both tests have exceptions. Up to 18% of pneumococci are optochin resistant, so bile solubility is the better tie-breaker, and lytA PCR is the reference.
Back to our patient. Rapid antigen tests are very specific but miss cases, especially when few bacteria are on the swab.
That is why a negative rapid test in a child or teen is backed up by culture or a rapid NAAT. Here the culture shows group A.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards appear in turn: “PYR-positive = group A” (✓ enterococci are PYR positive too — add bacitracin and salt/bile esculin); “A negative rapid strep rules out group A in a child” (✓ back up with culture or NAAT); “Optochin resistant = not pneumococcus” (✓ confirm with bile solubility or lytA PCR).

cues.text: Trap one: PYR positive means group A. Not alone. Enterococci are PYR positive too; add bacitracin, salt and bile esculin.
Trap two: a negative rapid strep rules out group A in a child. No. Back it up with culture or a rapid NAAT.
Trap three: optochin resistant means not pneumococcus. No. Some pneumococci resist optochin; confirm with bile solubility.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “β: A = bacitracin S + PYR + · B = CAMP + hippurate + · Enterococcus = PYR + salt + bile esculin”, “α: pneumococcus = optochin S + bile soluble · negative rapid strep in kids → culture/NAAT”.

cues.text: Sort catalase-negative cocci by hemolysis, then confirm: group A is bacitracin sensitive, group B is CAMP positive, Enterococcus grows in salt and bile, pneumococcus dissolves in bile, and a negative rapid strep in a child needs a backup test.

props.label: β: A = bacitracin S · B = CAMP + · Enterococcus = PYR + salt + bile esculin
α: pneumococcus = optochin S + bile soluble · negative rapid strep in kids → backup

explanation.what: Plain language: after catalase, read what the colony does to blood, then use a few disks and broths to name the organism. Scientific terms: β-hemolysis (clear halo, complete lysis), α-hemolysis (greenish halo, partial lysis), γ (no change). Group A (S. pyogenes): bacitracin sensitive, PYR positive. Group B (S. agalactiae): CAMP positive, hippurate positive, PYR negative. Enterococcus: PYR positive, grows in 6.5% NaCl, bile esculin positive. S. pneumoniae: α-hemolytic, optochin sensitive, bile soluble.
explanation.why: Bile salts trigger pneumococcal autolysis. The CAMP factor of group B acts with S. aureus sphingomyelinase (β-lysin) to lyse sheep red cells synergistically. Rapid antigen tests miss infections with few organisms on the swab.
explanation.measure: Bacitracin disk zone; PYR spot test (red = positive); CAMP streak perpendicular to S. aureus; hippurate hydrolysis; 6.5% NaCl broth; bile esculin; optochin (P) disk zone; bile solubility (tube or direct from blood culture); lytA PCR as reference for pneumococcus; Quellung reaction with type-specific antisera for serotyping.
explanation.differs: PYR is positive in both group A and Enterococcus: bacitracin and salt/bile esculin separate them. Pneumococcus vs viridans: optochin and bile solubility. Rapid antigen vs culture vs NAAT: specificity high, sensitivity lower for rapid antigen.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: PYR-positive organism with no bacitracin zone that grows in salt (Enterococcus), CAMP arrowhead (group B), optochin/bile pattern (pneumococcus), GBS screening window, and backup testing after a negative rapid strep in a child.

questions.stem: A blood culture grows catalase-negative Gram-positive cocci in pairs and chains. The isolate is PYR positive, shows no zone around a bacitracin disk, grows in 6.5% NaCl and blackens bile esculin. What is the most likely organism?

options.rationale: Correct. PYR positive with growth in 6.5% NaCl and a positive bile esculin test is the enterococcal pattern.
Incorrect. Group A is PYR positive but bacitracin sensitive, and salt tolerance points to Enterococcus.
Incorrect. Group B is PYR negative and is identified by CAMP and hippurate.
Incorrect. Pneumococcus is α-hemolytic, optochin sensitive and bile soluble, not salt tolerant.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with pharyngitis has a negative rapid group A antigen test. What should happen next?

options.text: Back up the result with a throat culture or a rapid NAAT
options.rationale: Correct. Rapid antigen tests are specific but less sensitive; negatives in patients aged 3–21 years are backed up.

options.text: Report group A as ruled out
options.rationale: Incorrect. A negative rapid antigen test can miss infection, especially with a light inoculum.

options.text: Repeat the same rapid antigen test until positive
options.rationale: Incorrect. Repeating a low-sensitivity test does not replace culture or NAAT.

options.text: Perform a CAMP test on the swab
options.rationale: Incorrect. CAMP identifies group B streptococci from colonies; it does not replace a backup test for group A.

questions.stem: α-Hemolytic, catalase-negative Gram-positive diplococci from CSF show no zone around an optochin disk. What is the best next step?

options.text: Test bile solubility (or lytA PCR) before ruling out S. pneumoniae
options.rationale: Correct. Some pneumococci are optochin resistant; bile solubility is the better tie-breaker and lytA PCR is the reference.
Incorrect. Optochin resistance alone does not exclude pneumococcus.
Incorrect. CAMP identifies group B, which is β-hemolytic.
Incorrect. Coagulase is for catalase-positive staphylococci.

references.citation: Gajic I, Jovicevic M, Kekic D, et al. Evolving approaches to bacterial identification: a review of classical and modern techniques. Int J Mol Sci. 2026;27(11):5092.
references.usedFor: Catalase separates Micrococcaceae (+) from Streptococcaceae (−); Enterococcus faecalis catalase −, bile esculin +, growth in 6.5% NaCl +, PYR +; S. pneumoniae α-hemolytic, catalase −, optochin sensitive, bile soluble (Tables 2 and 4).

references.citation: Gebre AB, Fenta DA, Negash AA, Hayile BJ. Prevalence, antibiotic susceptibility pattern and associated factors of Streptococcus pyogenes among pediatric patients with acute pharyngitis in Sidama, Southern Ethiopia. Int J Microbiol. 2024;2024:9282571.
references.usedFor: S. pyogenes is β-hemolytic (group A); β-hemolytic catalase-negative isolates that are bacitracin sensitive and PYR positive identified as S. pyogenes.

references.citation: Zhou J, Zhang L, Zhang Y, et al. Analysis of molecular characteristics of CAMP-negative Streptococcus agalactiae strains. Front Microbiol. 2023;14:1189093.
references.usedFor: CAMP factor of GBS enhances S. aureus β-hemolysin (sphingomyelinase) lysis of sheep red cells; long used for laboratory diagnosis of GBS; CAMP-negative strains exist.

references.citation: Guo D, Xi Y, Wang S, Wang Z. Is a positive Christie-Atkinson-Munch-Peterson (CAMP) test sensitive enough for the identification of Streptococcus agalactiae? BMC Infect Dis. 2019;19(1):7.
references.usedFor: Four of five confirmed S. agalactiae isolates were CAMP negative; a positive CAMP test lacks sensitivity for GBS.

references.citation: Shakir SM, Gill R, Salberg J, et al. Clinical laboratory perspective on Streptococcus halichoeri, an unusual nonhemolytic, Lancefield group B streptococcus causing human infections. Emerg Infect Dis. 2021;27(5):1309-1316.
references.usedFor: S. agalactiae is distinguished from group B-reacting S. halichoeri by S. halichoeri’s γ-hemolysis and negative hippurate hydrolysis (i.e., S. agalactiae is hippurate positive).

references.citation: Attaway C, Tobin E, Rhoads D. Answer to May 2024 Photo Quiz. J Clin Microbiol. 2024;62(5):e01194-23.
references.usedFor: S. halichoeri is discriminated from S. agalactiae by PYR positivity and hippurate negativity (i.e., S. agalactiae is PYR negative, hippurate positive).

references.citation: Devabhaktuni A, Silverman NS, Bastian IN, Turrentine MA. Trends in perinatal group B streptococcal disease after updated screening recommendations in the United States. O G Open. 2025;2(4):e094.
references.usedFor: ACOG (2019) moved universal prenatal GBS screening from 35 0/7–37 6/7 to 36 0/7–37 6/7 weeks of gestation; screening accuracy falls when collected > 5 weeks before birth.

references.citation: Aupaix A, Verroken A, Rodriguez-Villalobos H. Evaluation of a new protocol for rapid identification of Streptococcus pneumoniae in blood cultures using the modified bile solubility test: Gram staining is still standing. J Clin Microbiol. 2025;63(1):e0122224.
references.usedFor: Optochin separates S. pneumoniae from other α-hemolytic streptococci (resistant); optochin resistance in pneumococci up to 18%; some non-capsulated pneumococci bile insoluble and bile-soluble S. mitis described; bile solubility performs better than optochin; bile solubility based on pneumococcal autolysis; MALDI-TOF limited for S. mitis group; lytA PCR considered gold standard; Quellung reaction with serotype sera.

references.citation: Cohen JF, Chalumeau M, Levy C, et al. Spectrum and inoculum size effect of a rapid antigen detection test for group A streptococcus in children with pharyngitis. PLoS One. 2012;7(6):e39085.
references.usedFor: RADT specificity ≈ 95%, sensitivity ≈ 85% (range 65.6–98.9% in literature); sensitivity 95% with heavy vs 40% with light inoculum.

references.citation: Boyanton BL, Caldwell JM, Ledeboer NA. Review: current laboratory and point-of-care pharyngitis diagnostic testing and knowledge gaps. J Infect Dis. 2024;230(Suppl 3):S182-S189.
references.usedFor: IDSA: negative RADTs must be backed up by throat culture in patients aged 3–21 years (optional for others); FDA-cleared point-of-care NAATs approved without need for confirmatory culture.

references.citation: Fialho N, Marques JM, Barreto-Crespo MT, Semedo-Lemsaddek T. Cross-sector antimicrobial resistance and virulence in Enterococcus spp. from humans, animals and the environment. Antibiotics (Basel). 2026;15(7):657.
references.usedFor: Definitions: transparent halo = β, greenish halo = α (partial), no change = γ; β-hemolysis in 20.3% (15/74) of enterococcal isolates (horse blood, anaerobic).

claims.text: β = clear halo (complete lysis), α = greenish (partial), γ = none; most enterococci are not β-hemolytic.
Group A: β-hemolytic, bacitracin sensitive, PYR positive.
Group B: CAMP positive (CAMP factor + S. aureus sphingomyelinase), hippurate positive, PYR negative; CAMP-negative strains exist; screen at 36 0/7–37 6/7 weeks.
Enterococcus: catalase negative, PYR positive, grows in 6.5% NaCl, bile esculin positive.
S. pneumoniae: α-hemolytic, optochin sensitive, bile soluble by autolysis; up to 18% optochin resistant; some bile insoluble; MALDI weak on S. mitis group; lytA PCR reference; Quellung serotyping.
Rapid GAS antigen: specificity ≈ 95%, sensitivity ≈ 85%, ≈ 40% with light inoculum; negatives backed up at 3–21 years; POC NAATs need no backup culture.
Group B and enterococci are bacitracin resistant.
claims.note: Not taught as a stand-alone fact; no source read states it. The lesson separates group A from Enterococcus by bacitracin sensitivity plus salt and bile esculin.

claims.text: Schematic plates, zones, CAMP streaks and cocci.
“A zaps, B arrows, P pops, E endures.”

accuracyFlags.issue: Hit 29 calls Enterococcus a “bacitracin-resistant + PYR-positive β-hemolytic streptococcus”. Enterococcus is a separate genus and most isolates are not β-hemolytic (20% in one 2026 study). The lesson teaches salt and bile esculin confirmation.

morphology.note: Plates, hemolysis halos, zones, CAMP streaks and cocci are schematic drawings, not real culture images.

verification.notes: 6 claims checked against 11 open-access sources read for this lesson; 1 pending (bacitracin resistance of group B and enterococci). No human expert has reviewed this lesson.
